summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would abolish the independent body Health Workforce Australia (HWA).
HWA's functions and programmes would move to the Commonwealth Department of Health, and its assets, liabilities, contracts and other instruments would be transferred.
The government says the change would reduce duplication and bureaucracy and improve the delivery of health workforce policy.
changes: Transfers HWA's functions and programmes to the Commonwealth Department of Health.
Provides for the transfer of HWA's assets, liabilities, interests in land, records and instruments.
summary.affected: Health Workforce Australia and the Commonwealth Department of Health.

divisions.question: The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/debate/?id=2014-06-04.20.11) to read the bill for a second time.(Read more about the stages that a bill must pass through to become law [here](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ) This means that the majority agree with the main idea of the bill and that the House can now discuss it in more detail. _Background to the bill_ The bill was introduced to abolish the [Health Workforce Australia](https://www.hwa.gov.au/about-us) ('HWA'), which had been introduced by the [Council of Australian Governments](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Australian_Governments) "to address the challenges of providing a skilled, flexible and innovative health workforce that meets the needs of the Australian community".(Read more about HWA [here](https://www.hwa.gov.au/about-us).)

Jan McLucas I rise to speak on the Health Workforce Australia (Abolition) Bill and I want to indicate that the Labor Party will be opposing this bill. In the explanatory memorandum of this bill, it describes the purpose of the bill: It will enable more efficient and effective delivery of policy and programme activities related to the health workforce, to ensure Australia continues to have a high quality, capable and well distributed health workforce, delivering frontline health services for all Australians. That is simply not true. The word that I am offended by is the word 'continues'. We do not have a 'high-quality, capable and well-distributed health workforce' in this country. We do have a high-quality and capable health workforce, but frankly it has never been well distributed; that was why Labor in government established Health Workforce Australia. We received no substantial evidence at the Senate Community Affairs Legislation Committee inquiry that would support the contention that was included in the explanatory memorandum. In fact, the overwhelming evidence points to the success of Health Workforce Australia and its success into the future. Many witnesses who came before our committee said that the work had not yet been completed. So Labor will oppose this bill here in the Senate. In saying that, can I say that the motivation from the government is purely political and frankly spiteful. Labor established Health Workforce Australia through legislation in May 2009. This was partly in response to a Productivity Commission inquiry that was established in 2006. That was before Labor came to government, so the current government knows well and truly that our country has a problem in the distribution of our workforce. The Productivity Commission concluded that a more sustainable and responsive health workforce was needed. speeches.speaker: Peter Dutton
speeches.brief: Introduced the Health Workforce Australia (Abolition) Bill 2014, saying HWA duplicated Department of Health functions and that states and territories failed to provide their expected share of almost $540 million in funding, and that transferring its programs, including national workforce modelling, to the department would cut duplication without withdrawing support.

speeches.speaker: Amanda Rishworth
speeches.brief: Opposed abolishing Health Workforce Australia, noting 74 per cent of Australia faced a medical workforce shortage when Labor took office in 2007, and said the agency delivered over 8,400 new clinical training places across 22 disciplines and produced Australia's first national workforce projections in its 2012 Health Workforce 2025 report.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Opposed the Health Workforce Australia (Abolition) Bill, recalling that 74 per cent of Australians faced a GP workforce shortage when Labor took office in 2007, and noted the Commonwealth committed $1.38 billion under the national partnership agreement while states pledged a further $540 million toward workforce planning.

speeches.speaker: Peter Hendy
speeches.brief: Argued in support of abolishing Health Workforce Australia, noting the Commonwealth had been its sole funder, committing $1.05 billion since 2010 while states failed to contribute a promised $540 million, and said the budget would introduce a $7 GP co-payment from 1 July 2015 while increasing overall health spending from $64.5 billion to $74.8 billion by 2017 to 2018.

speeches.speaker: Catherine King
speeches.brief: Opposed the Health Workforce Australia (Abolition) Bill, noting the agency, established in 2009, has funded close to 8½ thousand new clinical training places across 22 disciplines and supported a 115 per cent increase in simulated education hours.

speeches.speaker: Kelvin Thomson
speeches.brief: Opposed the Health Workforce Australia (Abolition) Bill, noting Labor invested more than $344 million in the agency in the 2013 to 2014 budget, and argued nursing graduates are losing jobs to 457 visa holders, citing over 110,000 workers on 457 visas as of 31 March, up 5.9 per cent in a year, and an online petition with over 27,000 signatures calling for a visa review.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Opposed the Health Workforce Australia (Abolition) Bill, arguing it will return Australia to the boom-and-bust health workforce planning identified in the 2006 Blame Game report, noting the agency has funded 8,400 new clinical training placements across 22 disciplines and supported a 115 per cent increase in simulated education hours in 2012.

speeches.speaker: Julie Owens
speeches.brief: Opposed the Health Workforce Australia (Abolition) Bill, noting the 2008 national partnership agreement committed over $3 billion in combined funding, and highlighted a decline in GP proceduralists in regional and remote areas from 24 per cent in 2002 to 12 per cent in 2000 as evidence the workforce problem remains unresolved.

speeches.speaker: Stephen Jones
speeches.brief: Opposed the Health Workforce Australia (Abolition) Bill, citing a stark city-country divide of 220 specialists per 100,000 people in major cities versus 48 per 100,000 in the bush, recalled a 74 per cent medical workforce shortage when Labor took office in 2007, and warned university fee deregulation could push the cost of a medical degree from about $80,000 to between $100,000 and $183,000.

speeches.speaker: Lisa Chesters
speeches.brief: Opposed the bill abolishing Health Workforce Australia, citing data showing regional Victorians have a life expectancy 4.7 years lower than city residents and outer regional areas have only 43 specialists per 100,000 people compared with 134 in cities, and said $29 million will be cut from Bendigo electorate hospitals over five years.

speeches.speaker: Natasha Griggs
speeches.brief: Supported the bill abolishing Health Workforce Australia as red tape reduction, noted the Commonwealth has been its sole funder at $1.05 billion since 2008, and highlighted budget measures including doubling the Practice Incentive Program payment from $100 to $200 per teaching session and increasing GP training places by 300, from 1,200 to 1,500, in 2015.

speeches.speaker: Peter Dutton
speeches.brief: Defended the bill, said hospital funding will rise nine per cent, nine per cent and nine per cent over three years and six per cent in the fourth, noted the government inherited a health portfolio with 23 outside agencies, and quoted former Labor finance minister Tanner warning that indiscriminate creation of agencies jeopardises policy outcomes and raises fixed costs.
